entities.summary:
Peter Cellensis (c. 1115 – 1183), also known as Peter of Celle, was a prominent French Benedictine abbot, theologian, and bishop, whose intellectual and monastic leadership significantly shaped the spiritual and administrative landscape of the late 12th-century Latin Church. His career spanned key monastic houses, culminating in his elevation to the bishopric of Chartres, placing him at the intersection of spiritual reform and ecclesiastical governance during a period of intense intellectual ferment and papal consolidation. Peter’s extensive correspondence with figures like John of Salisbury and Thomas Becket provides invaluable insight into the philosophical, theological, and political concerns of his era, marking him as a crucial conduit for understanding the intellectual currents of the High Middle Ages.

Born around 1115, Peter entered the Benedictine order, eventually becoming abbot of Saint-Remi in Reims in 1162, after serving as abbot of the monastery of Montier-la-Celle near Troyes from 1145. At Saint-Remi, he undertook significant reforms, emphasizing strict monastic observance and intellectual pursuits, aligning with the broader Cistercian and Cluniac reform movements of the 12th century. His abbacy was marked by active participation in ecclesiastical councils and a prolific literary output, including numerous letters and theological treatises such as his 'De panibus' (On the Loaves) and 'De disciplina claustrali' (On Monastic Discipline). In 1181, he was appointed Bishop of Chartres, a major episcopal see, where he continued his administrative and pastoral work until his death in 1183.
